#11046. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1828 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • Recent findings suggest that that is embarrassing onstage.
  • Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

Recent findings suggest that that is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a newly introduced guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Sources indicate that standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

In a recent development, ⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

According to recent reports, A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

It has been revealed that this is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a upcoming source signal driving what gets written.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not fresh tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

According to recent reports, 2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

In a recent development, nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Recent findings suggest that mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Sources indicate that applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

It has been revealed that the sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

According to recent reports, if accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Sources indicate that great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially key as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

Sources indicate that on your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each latest task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ransomware group sets a deadline for the chipmaker to pay up - or see its data leaked.

Finding a new CEO is just one of their problems. Nvidia is investigating an alleged breach following claims by ransomware group The Gentlemen's affiliates that they hacked the AI giant and stole sensitive information.

It has been revealed that the embattled chipmaker told The Register's that it was investigating a possible third-party data breach. “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson noted. “We continue to monitor the situation.".

Industry observers note that the ransomware gang’s data-leak site, shared on social media and seen by The Register, doesn’t show any stolen files or indicate what information the group claims to have stolen. Nvidia first appeared on the criminals’ blog on Wednesday, with The Gentlemen promising “DATA INFO - SOON.”.

The post also included a countdown, ending November 28.

Recent findings suggest that while we can’t verify the criminals’ claims, the group, which emerged in mid-2025, is one of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service operations. Its affiliates claimed more than 320 victims as of April, with the majority of these alleged ransomware infections (240) occurring in the first half of 2026.

Industry observers note that the actual count, however, is likely much higher. Check Point researchers accessed an affiliate’s live command-and-control server during an incident response case earlier this year. The server contained victim telemetry that revealed more than 1,570 victims, mostly located in the US, and primarily corporate and organizational environments.

Industry observers note that according to an operational technology (OT) threat report from Trellix published on Wednesday, industrial ransomware claims jumped nearly 51 percent - to about 1,500 posts- compared to last quarter, and The Gentlemen’s affiliates were the most prolific claim posters during this time period. They accounted for about 16 percent of all posts.

In February 2022, an Nvidia data breach exposed employees’ credentials and proprietary code. Extortion crew Lapsus$ claimed to be responsible for that intrusion and data theft.®.

tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

📅 21 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows.
  • Industry observers note that as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift.
  • It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

Industry observers note that as models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

It has been revealed that this is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Recent findings suggest that before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

It has been revealed that we showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

It has been revealed that v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

According to recent reports, A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

Industry observers note that the model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

According to recent reports, the tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

According to recent reports, each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:.

Recent findings suggest that BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

It has been revealed that that regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

Recent findings suggest that A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Recent findings suggest that real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

In a recent development, naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. Fresh words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Reproduce the shared-prefix result with:.

Industry observers note that caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

In a recent development, the next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated latest memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

In a recent development, each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Sources indicate that repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

It has been revealed that both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

It has been revealed that the next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:.

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Industry observers note that every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

In a recent development, the benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage Presentations Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story.
  • In a recent development, jabez Eliezer Manuel discusses the 20-year evolution of Booking.com’s data management and ML platforms.
  • Jabez Eliezer Manuel brings two decades of software engineering experience to his role as Principal Engineer at Booking.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story.

In a recent development, jabez Eliezer Manuel discusses the 20-year evolution of Booking.com’s data management and ML platforms. He explains how they scaled MySQL topologies, sunset Hadoop for cloud architecture, and built high-throughput model serving and feature stores operating at 400B predictions per day. He also shares insights on personalization, interleaved experimentation, and their new agentic AI foundation.

Jabez Eliezer Manuel brings two decades of software engineering experience to his role as Principal Engineer at Booking.com. Over the past decade, he has tackled high-scale challenges ranging from low-latency search personalization to unified payment ledgers. Today, he drives the platform engineering for long-term agentic AI memory and next-gen intelligent application infrastructure.

According to recent reports, software is changing the world. QCon London empowers software development by facilitating the spread of knowledge and innovation in the developer community. A practitioner-driven conference, QCon is designed for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors, and project managers who influence innovation in their teams.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

In a recent development, jabez Eliezer Manuel: Today, Booking.com impacts billions of travel decisions, and behind each of those travel decisions is actually a bunch of ML platforms working behind the scenes. I'm here to talk about them. In the spirit of QCon's 20th anniversary, we are going to go back in time by two decades and take on a journey and then see how these platforms evolve.

It has been revealed that to make it easier for you to follow along, I've structured my talk into three layers, the data management layer, the ML engineering, and domain intelligence. In the data management layer, we will see the evolution of our databases, and some of the scale challenges that we had, and the cloud migration that we undertook to actually better our data. In the ML engineering layer, it'll be model serving at scale, and our feature engineering atoms there. In the domain intelligence layer, it'll be a high-level tour of all the machine learning platforms that we have. I'll pick one of them and then do a deep dive, so you get a full evolution of that specific platform, and you'll also have something tangible to take.

Let's go back to 2005. This was how the world looked like in 2005, if you remember these camera phones. Web 2.0 was taking off as a platform, and Booking.com was just like 9 years old. It had still not joined the Priceline group. Inside Booking, something fascinating was happening. We had run our first A/B experiment. Today everything goes through experimentation. It doesn't matter if it's a simple CSS change or an infrastructure change, everything goes through experimentation. At any point in time, if you're visiting Booking.com, you are subjected to 1,000-plus experiments, literally. Over the period of time, we have run 150,000 experiments or more until now. One thing that's certain is that most of our experiments fail, our success rate is just less than 25%. The goal isn't to get it right, but it is to learn fast. If you see that golden star on the top right, it's my little takeaway marker.

It's my way of hinting to you that there might be a lesson in this slide that is reusable for you. Continuing on experimentation. Experimentation built our data-driven DNA. It gave us a lot of technical benefits, which is sure. The ones that I like are that it eliminated HIPPOs. There were no endless debates internally. You just say, ok, let's go and build, test it, and done. The last is like, no, it created a culture of humility. There were no experts in the room, meaning that nobody could pinpoint and say, yes, let's experiment and then figure it out.

Experiments needed data, and that's where we are going to begin our journey in data management. In this part, I want to talk about our MySQL, our Hadoop, and our move to cloud. These are the three topics that I want to cover. This was our original tech stack when Booking.com started. It was just Perl and Postgres. Swiftly, we replaced Postgres with MySQL, primarily because of its asynchronous replication capabilities and for other reasons as well. In 2005, our setup was just a single master and four slaves. Fast forward 15 years, we were operating one of the largest clusters in the world. You might be wondering, how do you manage so many instances? Three things. We have a single writer setup, and we have replication chains, which I'll show you. Then we have a lot of automation. Let's make it real with an example, with an image. What you're seeing is a single master topology.

On the left, orange is the master, and then there are replicas or slaves. The colors indicate different data centers out there. As you can see, we minimize the replication across DCs by having intermediate masters. This whole topology is managed by a replication management tool called Orchestrator. If anybody is using MySQL, you might be aware of it. Automation was a necessity. For example, every 60 days, we take these 7,000 instances or so out, deprovision them, and reprovision them again. That meant that for every three minutes, there is some action that is going on. It is not humanely possible for some engineer to sit and do it. We have plenty of automation to do that.

There are a few things that makes our MySQL setup a little bit different. One is we don't use any specialized hardware. It's like simple frontend blades that are used for MySQL. No stored procedures, no UDFs, no views, not even a cache layer. Yes, no cache layers. The secret sauce, what we do is we actually create smaller DBs. The soft limit is 2 terabytes. The hard limit is 10 terabytes. We try to keep everything small. The reason is we want this database to fit into the fast storage of that server blade that we are using. In this example, we were normally using server blade 7 or 9, if you are aware of its configuration. What that meant is our point queries were less than 350 microseconds, which was roughly in the order of some of the memory engines out there. We were effectively using MySQL as a cache.

It also provided several side benefits. It was faster backups, quicker failovers, and primarily also lower cost, because if you're moving away from fast storage to iSCSI, it's expensive. We didn't just use MySQL. We actually helped shape it. What do I mean by that? Typically, for an A/B testing, we actually take the users and split them across two groups, and then we show different search results for them, which was coming from different ranking models. In interleaving, what we did was we didn't show two groups, we didn't split the groups, we just demonstrated the same results for all users.

Those results were coming from merged data, meaning we would train a couple of models, in this case, two models, red and blue. We trained the model, and each of these models gave a list of results. Then we would somehow need to merge it. One simple example could be, take the top one from here, top one from here, merge it. Then keep alternating it. It's just a team draft approach. Then once you have done, you present that to all people across the service. Then you check offline, ok, from which list did the user interact more? Was it from model A or from model B? That gives us the answer. Why it was useful was we could suddenly run more variants. On the right side, it doesn't have to be two. We can even run eight different models that are actually interleaving the results for search. That is, we can run more variants that was like 10 times speed-up than what we are used to with A/B testing.

According to recent reports, we could use it with less traffic because interleaving is super sensitive to customer preferences, and we can get signals faster. The way we use it now, interleaving and A/B, is that we train a bunch of models, we pre-select it with interleaving, we pick up a winner, and then we take the winner and then do proper A/B testing. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Security shop buys the hand that feeds it.

As AI has become a thorn in the side of the security industry, Palo Alto Networks (PAN) has reached an agreement to acquire Applied Compute, an AI model training platform.

"We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments," noted Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, during the company's fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Wednesday. "The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks.".

It has been revealed that so in the spirit of "hair of the dog that bit me," PAN is ingesting Applied Compute to make open-weight AI more secure for corporate customers. The answer to insecurity brought on by AI is buying security with AI.

In its announcement of the tie-up, PAN declares "the future of enterprise AI is hybrid, and that a large share of enterprises will run on open-source and open-weight models tuned to their own data, cost, and control needs.".

Sources indicate that that view has been clouded a bit by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's fall from grace: Back in July, he came to the defense of open-weight models as a defense against the hegemony of purveyors of closed-weight commercial models like Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. His resignation as CEO of Nvidia has led to worries that the open-weight ecosystem has lost some lobbying power at a time when the US is wary about the uptake of models made in China.

Nonetheless, PAN clearly sees a future for open-weight models.

Recent findings suggest that "Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, in a statement. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional.".

The firm expects the $4.5 billion all-stock transaction to add more than $1 billion to the company's Next Generation Security business by FY 2029.

Arora, on the firm's earnings call, explained the pricey bet as recognition of the corporate desire to avoid vendor lock-in and to retain control of data.

Industry observers note that "We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open-weight and open-source models," he mentioned. "Early signs of that shift are clear, with open-weight models growing from under 5 percent of token traffic to more than 60 percent over the past year.".

In a recent development, beyond the sticker price, PAN is ready to up its infrastructure ante. Arora remarked the biz expects to build infrastructure supporting more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity, a project that will take "a modest CapEx commitment of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030." ®.

First service outages, then data breaches…what's next?!

JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants.

Industry observers note that “Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday. “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week.”.

Mastercard also cited a third-party provider in an email sent to The Register following our questions about the alleged breach.

Industry observers note that “We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses - non-payments information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” Mastercard SVP Seth Eisen said. “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.”.

JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media.

In a recent development, “We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”.

According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.

“There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank noted on Thursday.

In a recent development, none of the three financial firms would comment on who the third-party providers are, when the breaches occurred, and what specific data was stolen. The Register will update this story as we learn more details about the intrusions.

Extortion crew n0n claimed responsibility for all three alleged hacks, posting the financial giants to its data-leak site on Monday. The group, believed to be based in Russia, emerged in September and posted 108 victims over its first month in operations. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs.
  • According to recent reports, running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is where we are right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

According to recent reports, running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:.

Recent findings suggest that this is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU.

Sources indicate that GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so people can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:.

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

In a recent development, no extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:.

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

It has been revealed that for models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:.

Industry observers note that transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Sources indicate that our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

According to recent reports, the llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

It has been revealed that llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:.

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):.

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

Sources indicate that transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for newly introduced architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

Industry observers note that that opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

Industry observers note that A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):.

According to recent reports, these changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

According to recent reports, the initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:.

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

In a recent development, we would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.

LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (581 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

💡 Key Takeaways
  • InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn.
  • Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.
  • Recent findings suggest that linkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn.

Nov 18, 2026 2 min read.

Recent findings suggest that linkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure. The deployment reduces daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20, lowers compute costs by 10%, and improves application runtimes by 14%, compared with its previous Magnet implementation.

Daily shuffle fetch failures decreased from approximately 750 to 20 (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

According to recent reports, linkedIn's offline data platform executes more than 300,000 Spark jobs daily across thousands of production nodes, consuming approximately 200 petabyte-hours of compute. As the company moves toward a unified Flink architecture for real-time and historical processing, large-scale backfills introduce additional shuffle workloads. Shuffle moves intermediate data between processing stages, potentially stressing networks, disks, and application runtimes.

In a recent development, linkedIn previously addressed shuffle read inefficiencies with Magnet, its push-based shuffle implementation contributed to Apache Spark 3.2. Magnet aggregates shuffle blocks by reducer partition into larger files, reducing random disk reads. However, shuffle storage remained within the compute cluster, where External Shuffle Services shared CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network resources with compute workloads.

With Apache Celeborn, map tasks push intermediate data to dedicated workers, which aggregate and store partitions independently of compute executors. Reducers fetch the data directly from these workers, allowing shuffle storage to scale independently of compute and reducing dependence on executor lifecycles. Unlike Magnet, which uses merger External Shuffle Services within the Spark compute cluster, Celeborn runs as a separate shuffle service with dedicated workers and a replicated control plane. This separation reduces resource contention between compute and shuffle workloads.

Celeborn architecture at LinkedIn (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post).

Aravind Patnam, a staff software engineer at LinkedIn, explained,.

Operating it reliably across thousands of nodes and hundreds of thousands of daily applications required substantial engineering beyond the upstream project.

The deployment uses a five-node Raft-based control plane distributed across availability zones, with Apache Ratis providing metadata replication, leader election, and failover. LinkedIn also introduced network-aware replication and integrated Celeborn with its host health platform to deprioritize workers approaching maintenance and exclude degraded workers. These changes contributed to a 20-fold reduction in task failures during infrastructure disruptions compared with Magnet.

Recent findings suggest that linkedIn further optimized the data plane by moving shuffle storage to NVMe SSDs, reducing overall shuffle duration by 40%. Using Zstandard compression instead of LZ4 reduced the required shuffle worker fleet by approximately 35%. The company also provisioned workers with 100 Gbps network interfaces and improved slot selection time sixfold through JVM and data-plane optimizations. Across the fleet, shuffle cost decreased by nearly 90% per task, while the proportion of executor runtime spent waiting on shuffle operations fell by approximately 10–15% from its peak.

The converged Flink platform processes hundreds of millions of events per hour in historical backfills, completing multi-day workloads in single-digit hours. Thousands of pipelines now use unified Flink computations for nearline processing and historical corrections, replacing parallel Spark implementations. LinkedIn is exploring caching and faster upstream upgrades while continuing to contribute to Celeborn.

Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bluesky's preferred encrypted messaging app allows multiple identities without tying you to a phone number.
  • The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.
  • "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bluesky's preferred encrypted messaging app allows multiple identities without tying you to a phone number.

The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.

"Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them.".

Building a fresh messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime.

In a recent development, "At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue remarked. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption.".

Xue noted the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering.

Sources indicate that germ Network's goal, remarked Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained.

Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network.

Industry observers note that "Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life.".

At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play.

Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content.".

Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore looks to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements.

Sources indicate that "I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device.".

If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success.

But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky.

Recent findings suggest that bluesky debuted Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose.

"On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app.

Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option.

At some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.
  • AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

Sources indicate that as AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

It has been revealed that this builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:.

It has been revealed that these results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve demonstrates the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

Industry observers note that when results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

Sources indicate that the EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

Sources indicate that the coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Industry observers note that once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

Quick history refresher: Nvidia tried to buy Arm for ~$40B back in 2020. The FTC sued 4-0 to stop it [ftc.gov] in Dec 2021, the UK and EU had their own investigations going, and Nvidia gave up in Feb 2022. SoftBank even got to keep the $1.25B Nvidia had already paid. The FTC's big complaint wasn't Nvidia owning the IP. This is why I care about open ISAs. I like the Arm ISA, really I do, but it's a product one organization rents out. Arm tried to make Qualcomm destroy the Nuvia core designs (and lost). And look at Apple: the userspace is plain AArch64, but everything around it is undocumented Apple-only weirdness. Custom interrupt controller, custom boot chain, secret GPU. Asahi has to reverse-engineer every latest chip, and M3 support only just landed this month, still with no GPU acceleration. That's the kind of lock-in an architecture license lets you build.

Recent findings suggest that RISC-V and Power are royalty-free, and there's no single company to buy, sue or headhunt. Until Arm is in that category, I'm backing RISC-V or Power ISAs and I'm staying on x86-64 ISA until one of those two open ISAs takes off. x86-64 isn't an open standard on paper, but the baseline (x86-64-v1) AMD Athlon 64 patents have expired, and x86 has 40+ years of inertia and a long line of non-Intel implementations behind it: Cyrix, Transmeta, VIA, Zhaoxin. Compaq clean-rooming the IBM BIOS is why the PC platform is open in the first place. Used x86-64 servers are a dime a dozen on eBay, and I can scrounge a working CPU pretty much anywhere on the planet, even on an island like Hawaii, without anybody's permission or a working supply chain.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization matter got Digital Ocean ducking.
  • If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.
  • According to recent reports, VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware notes means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization matter got Digital Ocean ducking.

If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.

According to recent reports, VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware notes means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite.

VMware also wants its people to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root.

According to recent reports, the prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software.

The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618).

VMware aims to ship newly introduced versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol.

Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours.

This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host.

It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

Sources indicate that this flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts customers of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5.

Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai notes the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

Yomtov states he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.

Yomtov and Terra Security rapidly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

In a recent development, the Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to patch its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

Sources indicate that terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.

The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that reinforcement Learning environments give newly introduced capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents.
  • An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome.
  • It has been revealed that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that reinforcement Learning environments give newly introduced capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

It has been revealed that an RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Recent findings suggest that every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, owners of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a latest paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

Sources indicate that we think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it.".

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

It has been revealed that the dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

In a recent development, the RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:.

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

Industry observers note that the viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

Recent findings suggest that the Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

Recent findings suggest that A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

In a recent development, neMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:.

Sources indicate that the bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your owners publish becomes visible to everyone else.

Recent findings suggest that if you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task.
