Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • It has been revealed that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

It has been revealed that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that looks, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the upcoming modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Recent findings suggest that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

It has been revealed that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

In a recent development, A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

Sources indicate that the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

In a recent development, use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Sources indicate that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

In a recent development, as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

Industry observers note that the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

It has been revealed that we tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning indicates up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:.

This is a massive model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

Sources indicate that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

Sources indicate that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

In a recent development, now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

In a recent development, the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

It has been revealed that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

In a recent development, muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

Recent findings suggest that we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

In a recent development, finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

Breaking: Farcall, a terminal-ready Rust PC+DOS emulator

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dialup

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, currently an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU.
  • According to recent reports, at the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt.
  • According to recent reports, coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, currently an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU. You can SSH into it and land in DOS, where you can experience fun programs including Zork, NetHack, GW-BASIC, Sopwith, and Digger Remastered.

Try it for yourself in your terminal:.

According to recent reports, at the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

According to recent reports, coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator? How hard could it be? I’d always assumed that writing an entire x86 emulator was a lot of work, but attending VCF gave me a hankering to learn more deeply how things work under the hood on computers in my vintage computing niche, but also the computers I use every day.

Recent findings suggest that in 1978, Intel released the 8086 chip that introduced the x86 architecture. The 1981 IBM Personal Computer used a variant, the 8088, and is the ancestor of PCs as we know them today. I picked up my very own early-model IBM PC a few years ago. It boots into PC-DOS, and runs programs off 5¼ inch floppy disks (mine has no hard drive). The Monochrome Display Adapter and the IBM 5151 monitor display its beautiful green-on-black text. The only input device is the famously clicky Model F keyboard.

An IBM PC, just like my own, that I saw recently at The National Museum of Computing in Bletchley Park, England.

Recent findings suggest that as a concrete target, I decided to emulate the 8088, as that’s the chip in my IBM PC. I am by far not the first person to do this—there are far more capable emulators for the IBM PC, including MartyPC, DOSBox, and 86Box. This was very much meant as a personal education mission for me.[1].

My first naive thought was that I needed to implement each of the instructions of the 8088. I knew I wanted it to boot DOS, run programs on it, and eventually boot Windows 3.1 (one of my favorite operating systems of the era). But I didn’t realize quite how much there would be to get to that point.

It has been revealed that I set out by trying to run COM files. COM is DOS’s simple executable format (you may recognize it from hits like COMMAND.COM, FORMAT.COM and indeed, WIN.COM if you ever typed “win” at the command line to start Windows). I started with a simple COM program that prints “Hello World” to the console as my first target.

My emulator, which I’m calling Farcall, started off very simply: a Rust command-line program running on my Mac, that reads in the bytes of a COM file from disk, and decodes and executes each instruction in a loop. Each instruction in the 8088 has an opcode byte (a number from 0x00 to 0xFF), optionally followed by more bytes.[2] (This is different from many RISC architectures like Arm64 where every instruction is the same width). For example:.

Farcall reads in the opcode (50, B0, or 83 above), and then however many additional bytes are necessary to interpret that type of instruction.

Sources indicate that if there were any opcodes that my emulator didn’t recognize, it would panic, and print out the unsupported opcode. I soon got into a rhythm: I would implement one instruction, run the program, and see where it next stopped. I just needed to do this ~300 more times, for each of the instruction forms.

To keep track of my todo list, I printed out the full list of instructions from Intel’s 8086 Family Users Manual, and put a blue check mark next to each instruction as I implemented it.

Even from my “Hello World”, I realized that it’s not enough to implement the CPU’s instructions. The x86 has an INT (interrupt) instruction that looks up an address in the interrupt vector table and calls the handler there. On the IBM PC, these handlers are typically set up by the BIOS or DOS. My “Hello World” used INT 21h to ask DOS to write a string to the screen, so in addition to implementing the CPU’s INT instruction, I had to also emulate the DOS service to write the string.

Recent findings suggest that once my Hello World COM program worked, I repeated this process a few more times with some other simple programs. And then I found out that Microsoft open-sourced some versions of MS-DOS a few years ago, so I set my sights on running MS-DOS 2.0’s MORE.COM (the pager), as my first “real” program. While it was a bit of a slog with all the instructions I had to implement, it was still an incredibly rewarding cycle–with each newly introduced instruction, the program would run just a bit more, and hundreds of instructions would fly across my screen as they were executed.

Recent findings suggest that I also implemented part of INT 10h—the BIOS’s Video service, which MORE.COM uses to learn about the current screen dimensions, etc. So now I was emulating a small subset of yet another layer, the BIOS. With that, though, MORE.COM ran properly—a DOS program seemingly running in the macOS terminal.

My eventual goal is to run Windows 3.1 on Farcall. However, one of the many steps before that is to get DOS to boot, since Windows 3.1 runs on top of it.

It has been revealed that in order to do that, I knew that I needed to deal with boot sectors—some code at the beginning of a disk that typically loads an operating system. I own a bunch of 5¼ inch floppy disks that came with my IBM PC with software for it. I took an image of my PC-DOS 2.0 floppy, and added a “boot” mode to the emulator that would take an image and execute its boot sector, instead of a COM file.

When a PC boots from a floppy, the BIOS reads the first sector (512 bytes) into memory and executes the instructions in it. On my PC-DOS diskette, those instructions start loading DOS. Methodically, I implemented even more of the 8088’s instructions (about 200 more), and several interrupts that a BIOS would normally listen for, including keyboard support, video handling (the simplest 80x25 text mode), and reading from a floppy disk. With some persistence, I got to the point where the boot sector transferred control to the system files (IBMBIO.COM and IBMDOS.COM), and eventually to COMMAND.COM.

Getting DOS to boot was a bit of a relief—before this point my emulator was performing the work of the CPU, the BIOS, and DOS; now I could stop handling INT 21h myself and let the emulation run DOS’s real handler.

Sources indicate that it also opened up the kinds of programs I could run. Multiplan, a spreadsheet program from 1982 (Microsoft’s answer to VisiCalc, the world’s first “killer app”) was the first one I got running, by implementing a bunch more instructions, and supporting 16-color text mode to let Multiplan's beautiful magenta-on-blue palette shine through.

So far I had been emulating a BIOS by intercepting interrupts to e.g. the Video, Keyboard, and Disk services. This was easier for me to get started, because in the emulator code I have free rein over memory and the CPU’s registers and I can talk directly to the frontend, and I can write only the specific missing pieces until things work.

According to recent reports, however, it was also limiting—the subset I’d built was just enough to boot DOS 2.0 and 3.3, but there are a lot more BIOS services, each with its own quirks and features, and the ones I had weren’t enough to boot FreeDOS, for instance. And around the same time, I discovered GLaBIOS, a modern and open-source BIOS implementation that runs on real IBM PCs.

While using someone else’s BIOS sounds easier than emulating one, it actually increased the scope of the emulator quite a bit: to support an actual BIOS ROM, you now need to emulate all the hardware the BIOS expects to talk to! This was where my naivety became clearer—I didn’t realize just how much peripheral hardware is inside an IBM PC. I knew there was a floppy drive, video card, and keyboard, of course, but I didn’t realize there’s also a Programmable Peripheral Interface (PPI), Programmable Interval Timer (PIT), and a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller.

It has been revealed that there’s a lot I had to learn about how each of these peripherals work together. For instance, I didn’t know that the floppy disk controller works with the DMA controller to read data from a disk into memory. Thankfully, there are some great resources like the MartyPC PC Emulation Book, the datasheets for the Intel chips, and previous versions of MIT’s 6.828 course website.

In a recent development, I eventually implemented enough of each of these devices that I got GLaBIOS to boot. Seeing the BIOS go through its POST sequence, and then deposit me at the DOS prompt, gave me a great sense of satisfaction. And now, because the devices were actually implemented, I could focus on improving the fidelity of the graphics.

It has been revealed that until then, I’d only supported text output, which is all that my own IBM PC can do, since it has the Monochrome Display Adapter. But the video card can be upgraded, like to one that supports CGA, known for its iconic color palettes like magenta-cyan-white. I decided I wanted to add CGA’s graphics mode so I could run programs with color graphics.

To do this, I needed to convert the bytes that programs write to video memory into RGB pixels for the Farcall frontend. Quite naturally, I expected the horizontal lines of pixels, or scanlines, to be stored in order: 0, 1, 2, 3. Here’s what Sopwith looked like when I interpreted video memory that way:.

Sopwith, when reading video memory lines contiguously.

Both the monochrome and color graphics cards are built around the Motorola MC6845 chip, a Cathode Ray Tube Controller (CRTC). This controller was designed around rows of text. As it draws the screen, the CRTC outputs two numbers: a memory address that tells the card where to fetch the current character, and a scanline number to select which horizontal slice of that character to draw.

It has been revealed that for 320x200 graphics, IBM couldn’t simply set the CRTC to output 200 rows of one scanline each, because the register that sets the number of character rows is only 7 bits wide, so it maxes out at 127. Instead, the engineers configured it to return 100 rows of 2 scanlines each, and wired the CRTC’s two outputs to build the address at which each pixel’s data could be found in video memory.

In a recent development, CGA has 16 KiB of video memory, split into two 8 KiB halves. The card uses the CRTC’s memory address to select a location within one of those halves. Both scanlines in a pair use the same relative location, but the card wires the scanline number (0 or 1) to bit 13 of the final address. Because 213 = 8192, the second scanline starts 8 KiB after the first. So the first half of memory holds scanlines 0, 2, 4, and so on, and the second half holds 1, 3, 5, etc. Once the scanlines are interpreted that way, Sopwith looked correct:.

Sopwith, reading video memory correctly with 8 KiB offset.

It has been revealed that I started Farcall as a terminal program that could run COM files in my macOS terminal. There was something attractive about seeing an old DOS program running in a modern terminal, as opposed to in a graphical window like a normal VM hypervisor.

This worked great for text-mode programs, but I wanted to go further to see if I could render CGA graphics-mode programs directly in the terminal too. I learned that the terminal emulator I use, Ghostty, supports the Kitty graphics protocol, which allows terminal applications to display inline images. I figured I could try using this to stream each frame from the guest’s video memory. And it turns out this works—though it feels like it’s at the edge of what the protocol and Ghostty’s implementation are meant to support. (e.g. I found I could reliably crash Ghostty when sending zlib frames, and a change in a recent version of Ghostty made frames flicker).

According to recent reports, now that I could display graphics-mode programs like Sopwith in the terminal, I wanted to share this experience of “running DOS in your terminal” with others, so I decided to put an installation of my emulator on a public SSH server. An increasing number of iconic DOS programs of the era are now being made open source by their owners (including MS-DOS itself as I mentioned, but also programs like GW-BASIC, Zork, and Sopwith), so I decided to put those in the environment for anyone to try.

It has been revealed that as I was preparing to launch the SSH service, one glitch I needed to solve was that of performance. Even though I was emulating a processor operating at 4.77 MHz on a VPS with a shared CPU supposedly running at 2.4 GHz, I was only able to fit 6 or so instances of Farcall running Sopwith per core before the emulation started dropping frames.

There were a couple things that were contributing to unnecessary CPU usage. Firstly, before every step of the emulation, I was checking the clock to see if it was time to pause emulation and handle some input/draw the screen. In profiling the code using a sample program, I found that fetching monotonic time (Instant::now() in Rust) was actually using ~43% of CPU time. Making the loop only check every 128 steps removed this bottleneck. (Note that this didn’t change the fact that the emulator is nowhere near cycle-accurate, or properly emulating how long each instruction or hardware operation takes; I’m pretending that every instruction takes equal time, for example).

In a recent development, another culprit was in my Kitty graphics code. Each frame is sent down as a separate PNG image.[3] At first I was sending full-color RGB PNGs, which was contributing to a significant amount of CPU usage in preparing each frame. However, by switching to 4-bit indexed (palette) images (which works perfectly given that you can only use one of 16 colors in CGA in normal circumstances[4]), I was able to save more than 70% of CPU time in preparing the frames.

According to recent reports, I was surprised just how much I’ve learned from this project in such a short period of time. I’ve been using computers since the 90s and am familiar with words like IRQs, DMA, and Cylinders/Heads/Sectors—but it wasn’t until I had to implement them in software that I truly appreciated them for what they are. It was also a fantastic refresher for how CPUs work at the instruction level, which feels a lot more concrete now. On the other hand, I was not ready for how quickly “emulating a CPU” ballooned into “emulating a whole computer including all its peripherals”.

Industry observers note that as for what’s next: My emulator is far from complete, and I still have a goal of running Windows 3.1. Probably the biggest hurdle in the way is support for protected mode, and emulating a 286. (Windows 3.0 is easier to run in this regard, since it supports the 8088, and still supported real mode). Even before that, I need to support hard drives, as well as a newer graphics mode like EGA or VGA. There’s a lot to do—but I look forward to learning a lot more about how computers work along the way!

You can try out Farcall yourself on a standard SSH client. You will unlock the full graphical experience on terminal emulators that support Kitty graphics like Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2, and Konsole.

In a recent development, at the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

Recent findings suggest that the source code is licensed under the MIT license and is available at https://github.com/keito/farcall. Provenance of the programs on the SSH server is available here.

According to recent reports, I wrote the code for the emulator by hand. I used Codex to help write unit tests and some test programs, and perform research. ↩.

An opcode is optionally preceded by one or more prefixes, which can do things like repeat the instruction. ↩.

I initially sent zlib-compressed pixels, but it kept crashing Ghostty, caused by a bug in the Zig DEFLATE library, so I switched to sending PNG images. This bug is fixed in the latest Ghostty after they switched to Wuffs. ↩.

Separately, two BIS licenses authorize various chips, including the H200, for Lenovo but exclude locations in China. Industry observers note that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.

These products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor. Products marked Vulnerable have no fixed release yet: every current version is vulnerable.

Updated 20 November 2026 at 09:29 UTC.

Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

It has been revealed that install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.

Sources indicate that most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).

Industry observers note that the output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

The same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.

UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.

A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.

We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then.

Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the first to demonstrate remote code execution.

The Ruby security advisory also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

In a recent development, we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

According to recent reports, alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

In a recent development, the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

Industry observers note that while still trailing frontier open-weight models, the newly introduced release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

According to recent reports, we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 highlights strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

In a recent development, apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

In a recent development, the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Sources indicate that structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Industry observers note that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

Recent findings suggest that the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been unveiled by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

Recent findings suggest that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

Industry observers note that if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.

Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

At QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

The talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he showed how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

To illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

The first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries upcoming tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

The second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With fresh people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

The third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a proposal and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

It has been revealed that the talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

The results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

Sources indicate that the presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, mitiga launched AI Agent Security on November 19, 2026, and made the agentless platform immediately available.
  • Agents can read data, call APIs, change records and trigger other agents using service accounts, OAuth grants, API tokens, workload identities or delegated sessions.
  • The platform establishes behavioral baselines around the systems agents access, the actions they perform and the identities they use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, mitiga launched AI Agent Security on November 19, 2026, and made the agentless platform immediately available. It is designed to discover and monitor AI agents across cloud, software-as-a-service (SaaS) and identity systems, then contain suspicious activity through customers’ existing security integrations.

Agents can read data, call APIs, change records and trigger other agents using service accounts, OAuth grants, API tokens, workload identities or delegated sessions. Co-founder and chief technology officer Ofer Maor described the resulting visibility problem: “An agent doesn’t need to break in when it already holds the credential. To the audit log, it looks like a valid login.”.

The platform establishes behavioral baselines around the systems agents access, the actions they perform and the identities they use. It compares live activity with permissions and static configuration to surface privilege drift and unauthorized access, then correlates cloud, SaaS, identity and AI activity into a unified incident record. Activity Flow maps customers and non-human identities through AI platforms and connectors to the applications they reached.

No gateway, SDK, proxy or code change inside an agent is required. Mitiga instead works from logs and APIs that supported platforms already produce, allowing deployment outside the agent’s execution path. Retained logs can also support investigations into agent activity that occurred before the platform was deployed.

Coverage spans homegrown agents built on services such as Bedrock and Azure AI Foundry, sanctioned vendor agents connected through OAuth grants, and employee-connected coding assistants, personal AI tools and unreviewed MCP servers or skills. Mitiga’s four named scenarios are third-party agent compromise, homegrown-agent overreach, coding-agent and MCP supply-chain threats, and cascading actions in which one compromised agent triggers tools, services or other agents.

For coding-agent supply-chain risks, the free Skillgate scanner checks skills and MCP servers for hidden instructions or credential-exfiltration paths before an agent acts. If the agent has already run, Mitiga reconstructs what the developer’s credentials did next.

According to recent reports, mitiga reports three operating figures: 95% of security-operations-center workflows automated, 100% of alerts triaged with an auditable verdict, and under three minutes from event collection through triage to an actionable response. The underlying Cloud Security Data Lake normalizes telemetry from more than 50 platforms and retains it for more than 1,000 days.

In a recent development, the product documentation explicitly distinguishes Mitiga from an inline guardrail: it does not block an action before that action occurs. Detection latency depends on the telemetry source, and coverage is limited to agents whose actions appear in supported cloud, SaaS, identity or AI sources.

In a recent development, prompt-level signals are available only where supported platform logs expose them, including Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, Agentforce and Copilot logs. Without that visibility, Mitiga detects the resulting downstream behavior.

According to recent reports, supported responses include revoking a token or session, quarantining an identity and reversing a change through customer integrations. Reversal depends on what each integration supports. For enterprises deploying the platform, log coverage and integration support therefore form part of its effective security boundary, determining where Mitiga can investigate an agent’s activity and which containment actions are available.

In a recent development, miles Okada is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence and cybersecurity with a focus on emerging threats, defensive architectures, and the evolving dynamics between attackers and automated systems. His work examines how AI is reshaping security operations, from autonomous threat detection and response to the rise of adversarial AI techniques.

Sources indicate that with a technical and investigative perspective, Miles analyzes security research, incident disclosures, and real-world deployments to understand where AI strengthens defenses—and where it introduces new vulnerabilities. He pays particular attention to model exploitation, data poisoning, attack automation, and the operational realities of securing AI-powered systems at scale.

Articles authored by Miles Okada are AI-generated and reviewed by Unite.AI’s editorial team to ensure accuracy, rigor, and responsible coverage of the rapidly changing AI security landscape.

Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
  • Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
  • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the upcoming US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Sources indicate that beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

In a recent development, the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types).

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

In a recent development, attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

It has been revealed that the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

Recent findings suggest that the router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

It has been revealed that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

Sources indicate that the residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Sources indicate that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

According to recent reports, the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Proposal for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

Industry observers note that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Industry observers note that beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Recent findings suggest that pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Recent findings suggest that beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

Sources indicate that for faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

According to recent reports, beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

According to recent reports, on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

Sources indicate that we are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

Industry observers note that * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

It has been revealed that training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

In a recent development, reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can patch the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the latest weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Sources indicate that optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one upgrade behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

Industry observers note that you can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

It has been revealed that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

Industry observers note that at Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

Sources indicate that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Industry observers note that our score-versus-latency plot highlights the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

Sources indicate that we wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Breaking: AWS Enables Default Monitoring for SageMaker AI Inference Endpoints

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Web Services (AWS) enabled default monitoring for eligible Amazon SageMaker AI generative AI inference endpoints on November 19, 2026, adding AWS Health findings for latency drift, idle GPU capacity and missed serving optimizations.
  • The monitoring requires no setup on endpoints that use vLLM serving containers and GPU instances.
  • In a recent development, the announcement extends the optimized generative AI inference recommendations that AWS introduced on April 22, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services (AWS) enabled default monitoring for eligible Amazon SageMaker AI generative AI inference endpoints on November 19, 2026, adding AWS Health findings for latency drift, idle GPU capacity and missed serving optimizations.

The monitoring requires no setup on endpoints that use vLLM serving containers and GPU instances. It reads endpoint-level latency, GPU utilization and serving configuration, not request or response content. The target is gradual drift after deployment as traffic, prompt lengths, serving software and model resource requirements change.

In a recent development, the announcement extends the optimized generative AI inference recommendations that AWS introduced on April 22, 2026. That workflow lets customers choose cost, latency or throughput as the objective, compare up to three instance types, and benchmark configurations on real GPUs with NVIDIA AIPerf. It also supports benchmarks of existing production endpoints; the newly introduced layer adds ongoing observation and notifications to that user-initiated decision process.

Latency-drift findings compare median (p50) end-to-end latency and median time to first token with the endpoint’s own preceding week. Because the baseline is historical, users do not need to set a threshold in advance. A resulting benchmark tests tensor parallelism settings and alternative instance types or sizes.

Other findings cover GPUs that remain well below capacity, supported but disabled speculative decoding, untuned GPU kernels, and serving containers missing newer performance improvements or patches for critical and high-severity vulnerabilities. For unused capacity, the benchmark tests cheaper instance types and smaller sizes at observed peak traffic. Configuration tests compare the current setup with speculative decoding enabled, tuned kernels or an updated container, as applicable.

AWS’s examples are walkthrough illustrations, not fleet-wide measurements: one reports median time to first token rising about 200 milliseconds week over week, while another reports even the busiest GPU using 12% or less of capacity for most of a week.

Findings arrive through AWS Health and email. Each endpoint gets at most one notification at a time covering all applicable findings, AWS limits how many an account receives at once, and notifications are specific to the endpoint’s AWS Region.

A notification states what was observed, why it matters for latency, capacity or cost, and a recommended action, with estimates labeled as estimates. It is an observation rather than a completed benchmark. The action opens an agentic experience in SageMaker Studio with the endpoint and its observed traffic prefilled.

After the user confirms, the agent generates an editable SageMaker Python SDK notebook using the endpoint’s model and a traffic profile derived from its metrics. The notebook tags the recommendation job with the AWS Health event so results can be traced to the finding. The job compares the current configuration with alternatives on response time, throughput and cost per million tokens, using separate compute; production does not change until the user applies a result.

Recent findings suggest that AWS recommends applying a selected configuration to one production variant first while keeping the existing configuration available for rollback. Holding or dismissing a finding is also a normal outcome, and the notification remains in AWS Health event history.

In a recent development, monitoring carries no additional GPU cost. Benchmarks use standard SageMaker AI charges or an existing machine-learning reservation, and acting on a finding requires a SageMaker Studio domain, AWS Identity and Access Management permissions to run recommendation jobs and update endpoints, and sufficient benchmark-instance quota.

According to recent reports, customers can manage delivery through AWS User Notifications and optionally schedule recurring recommendations, such as monthly runs. Setting the OPT_OUT_TRACKING environment variable on a model container stops collection of that endpoint’s engine metrics, GPU metrics and startup configuration details, and prevents its notifications.

Support for an optimization does not guarantee a benefit. AWS claims speculative-decoding results depend on concurrency and prompt and response lengths and can differ between peak and off-peak traffic. That distinction defines the feature’s practical role: default telemetry supplies the warning, while the benchmark determines whether a possible saving or speedup holds at the traffic that matters.

And what he then did is sequence the dog's DNA. You know, this is a guy with no biology background, sequenced the dog's DNA, and figured out what was wrong in the DNA that caused the cancer, developed an mRNA vaccine with AlphaFold.

The most expensive part of the experiment apparently was to actually synthesize the vaccine. And then he administered it to his dog; he had to get permission for that. And Rosie's tumors shrank, and she's is still here and is still hanging out and playing ball with this machine learning engineer.

Industry observers note that so I love this story, and this is why I love AI. Because I think if it can unlock the potential benefits, that is amazing. I want those benefits.
