AI Coding Agents Leak Thousands of Secrets to GitHub

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.
  • AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.
  • In a recent development, research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A command in Claude Code inadvertently saves files with credentials and other sensitive data to public Git repositories, creating security gaps for organizations.

AI coding assistants may inadvertently be leaking thousands of secrets to GitHub public repositories, making what seem like routine interactions between developers and these tools a gaping enterprise security risk.

In a recent development, research from security firm Apiiro found 2,539 credentials across nearly 2,000 public GitHub repositories, with secrets such as database passwords, cloud keys, API tokens, and SSH root logins among the exposed data, according to a recent report published online. Apiiro tracked some of the leaked data to Claude Code, which was, unbeknownst to people, copying secrets to a hidden file and committing them with the rest of the developer's code.

Among specific secrets leaked were "a database vendor's own admin-level cloud key, a production Azure Postgres password, a Square production token, and the owner password of a medical-records database," Apiiro researchers Shmulik Cohen and Matan Giladi wrote in the post.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering.

Most of the secrets belong to individual developers across 63 organizations, "from student groups to startups, software agencies, and established vendors," they wrote.

The issue stems from how coding assistants — Claude Code, in a specific case that the researchers examined — carry out certain commands. "Ask Claude Code to check a database or call an API, and the command it proposes carries the secret from your config file," the researchers explained.

The tool will ask the user before running the command and, if the choice is "Yes, and don't ask again," then "it saves that exact command, secret included, to .claude/settings.local.json inside the project folder," according to the report.

"Nothing in the repo marks that file as private, so it gets committed with the rest of the code," the researchers explained.

The fact that a routine development task creates a security exposure is dangerous for organizations, especially because these AI coding tools are supposed to be helpful, not harmful, notes Ryan McCurdy, vice president of marketing for database security firm Liquibase.

It has been revealed that “A developer approves a command to save time, the AI agent retains credentials as part of that approval, and those credentials can eventually end up in a public repository," he observes via email. "Nobody intended to expose them, but the workflow made it possible.".

In the case of Claude Code, Apiiro examined 104,185 publicly accessible copies of .claude/settings.local.json on GitHub, finding that 1,122 files contained real secrets. The researchers identified 1,379 distinct secrets in those files alone, including 636 provider-specific keys and 743 passwords or tokens associated with public hosts.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool.

Recent findings suggest that claude Code is not being overtly careless; it does try to protect files when it creates its .claude/settings.local.json file inside a Git repository, the researchers noted. The tool does this by adding the file to the developer's global Git ignore list, which tells Git to ignore the file on that particular developer's machine. This prevents it from being included in routine commits.

It has been revealed that however, the protection is not built into the development project itself, and the "ignore" rule does not travel with the repository when it is cloned onto another machine, the researchers noted. "The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it," they wrote.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, Claude Code itself was sometimes responsible for committing the exposed files. In 539 of the 1,105 repositories containing real secrets that the researchers investigated, a commit co-authored by Claude Code had modified the affected settings file.

The action that exposes these secrets while using Claude Code appears to be a "dead zone" of sorts for developers using AI coding assistants, so they likely have no idea that they've just exposed a secret, observes Seemant Sehgal, founder and CEO of AI penetration testing firm BreachLock.

Related:Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks.

In a recent development, "A 'don't ask again' prompt is a decision to write a credential into a file, and many developers clicking it likely don't know that file exists," he notes. "Once it lands in a repository, it sits in a place many secret scanners were never built to check, which appears to be why some of these leaks slipped through.".

Apiiro contacted Anthropic about the issue before publishing the findings. After their publication, Boris Cherny, Anthropic's head of Claude Code, mentioned in public comments that although Claude Code historically has not done secrets scrubbing, the company is looking into what it can do to prevent the secrets exposure described by Apiiro, according to Apiiro's report.

Those approaches may be to make sure auto mode catches the exposure, or to build in basic secrets scanning, among other ideas that Anthropic will prototype "to understand the tradeoffs" before shipping something with its next version of Claude Code, Cherny remarked.

Indeed, the leakage exposes how Claude Code's protection relies heavily on a developer-specific Git setting rather than a safeguard built into the project or the AI coding tool itself, exposing a gap that can turn an ordinary command approval into a persistent credential leak.

According to recent reports, to avoid this, Apiiro recommends that developers rotate every credential a file has ever held, and open all fields and delete every rule containing a secret, even if a file was never committed to a project. Meanwhile, security teams should treat all AI agent folders as secret-bearing on laptops as well as in repos, and add them to pre-commit and secret scanning, including history.

Industry observers note that "As AI agents become more involved in software development, organizations need to recognize that source code isn't the only thing they need to secure," McCurdy observes. "Agent configuration files, transcripts, and execution histories can contain sensitive information, and traditional security checks may not catch everything.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this upcoming generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

In a recent development, support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too massive to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Recent findings suggest that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

It has been revealed that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#10948. We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1252 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Violetpixel ↗ Open Full Page

We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Violetpixel

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit.
  • It has been revealed that when I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are.
  • The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST.

Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.

It has been revealed that when I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.

The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:.

Industry observers note that those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure.

Sources indicate that now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.

Recent findings suggest that and collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365, Air Traffic Control, United Airlines' systems, the NSA's network, many major banks, Apple's systems, and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.

I guess that depends on how you look at it.

I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.

Sources indicate that capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.

Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.

People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?

It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics.

Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this.

It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real.

It has been revealed that thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system).

We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a significant problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail.

Sources indicate that I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now.

Unfortunately, we're all getting burned.

Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • Recent findings suggest that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Recent findings suggest that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch people had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

It has been revealed that to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a upcoming backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Industry observers note that transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Sources indicate that models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

In a recent development, the bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

In a recent development, decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

Recent findings suggest that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

Industry observers note that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an matter on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an matter and tell us about it.

AWS Lets AgentCore Agents Buy Marketplace Products Through AWS Billing

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Web Services declared on November 19, 2026 that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments can now settle purchases from x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers through AWS Billing.
  • In a recent development, for those purchases, the integration removes the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys.
  • Sources indicate that A purchase starts when an agent calls a seller endpoint without payment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Web Services declared on November 19, 2026 that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments can now settle purchases from x402-enabled AWS Marketplace sellers through AWS Billing. AI agents can buy software, APIs, data and content per request in US dollars, with charges added to the agent developer’s AWS bill.

In a recent development, for those purchases, the integration removes the need for stablecoin wallets or API keys. An optional AWS Marketplace connector for AgentCore Gateway also lets agents discover paid products and endpoints, while developers keep spending limits, seller permissions and audit records within their AWS accounts.

Sources indicate that A purchase starts when an agent calls a seller endpoint without payment. The seller responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required and places a signed quote in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header. The agent forwards the quote to AgentCore payments through the ProcessPayment API using the AWS_BILLING_X402 payment type. If the session has enough remaining budget, the service returns a payment token; the agent retries the request with that token in the PAYMENT-SIGNATURE header and receives the content.

At launch, AWS Billing supports the x402 exact scheme, under which the seller quotes a fixed price for each request. AWS Marketplace verifies the quote’s signature against the seller’s registered key, rejecting a quote whose price has been altered. The post says payment tokens remain valid for about five minutes, so the quote, payment and redemption steps occur in a single pass.

The first purchase from a seller creates an AWS Marketplace agreement for the developer’s AWS account, and later purchases are tracked against it. Products appear as Marketplace line items, with settlement running asynchronously before charges appear on the monthly AWS bill. Purchases are also recorded in AWS CloudTrail and AWS Cost Explorer.

Setup requires a Payment Manager with an AWS Billing connector and an AWS Marketplace service-linked role. For each task, developers can create a payment session with a spending limit and give the agent its session ID. If the remaining budget is insufficient, the payment call fails and the developer is not charged.

AgentCore policy supports additional spending limits and approved-seller lists. Organizations using Private Marketplace restrict agents to the products that private catalog allows. The open-source sample also separates permissions: its session role can set budgets but cannot pay, while its agent role can pay but cannot create sessions, preventing the agent from increasing its own budget.

According to recent reports, the optional gateway connector exposes three read-only tools: search listings, get a listing and list fulfillment options. Listing search returns only endpoints that accept x402, while the fulfillment call supplies the seller’s endpoint URL and accepted payment protocols. Developers can bypass discovery by setting a seller URL directly; the agent then pays only that endpoint.

AWS’s walkthrough uses a Strands research agent answering a financial analyst’s question about agentic-payment announcements outside the model’s training data. The agent finds Tavily’s live-search listing, requests its x402 endpoints, obtains a quote and pays for one request. Its answer includes sources and identifies what it purchased and how much it cost.

In a recent development, the sample defaults to a $0.05 session budget and a $0.02 cap per request. In AWS’s documented test, the agent compared two listings before completing one $0.01 payment.

According to recent reports, for AWS customers, the launch connects product discovery and per-request payment to established cloud billing and governance controls. An agent’s purchasing autonomy is therefore bounded by the specific session budget, approved sellers, role permissions and Marketplace catalog access its developers configure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tanium introduced AgentSight at its Converge conference in Las Vegas this week, giving security teams a way to inventory AI software running on employee devices.
  • That launch is narrower than the long-term product Tanium described.
  • An enterprise can govern a tech giant-wide AI subscription and still have limited visibility into the assistants staff install on their own workstations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tanium introduced AgentSight at its Converge conference in Las Vegas this week, giving security teams a way to inventory AI software running on employee devices. The company states the first capabilities are available now in the Tanium console. They identify local models, coding agents, AI extensions and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers across Windows, macOS and Linux, then associate each item with a device and the person who installed it.

That launch is narrower than the long-term product Tanium described. The first release answers what is installed and where. The manufacturer is still developing parts of the system that would explain what an agent did, flag unusual behavior or apply a policy across many devices. For organizations choosing how to govern AI, the distinction matters: a complete inventory is valuable, but it does not establish that an agent’s actions are authorized.

An enterprise can govern a tech giant-wide AI subscription and still have limited visibility into the assistants staff install on their own workstations. An approved coding tool might sit alongside several extensions, a local model and a connector to another service. A software inventory lets IT see which devices are running those components and gives security staff a starting point for tracking down who installed them. It also helps explain why approving one service does not automatically account for every tool that ends up in a workflow.

It has been revealed that tanium notes its initial visibility is available in on-premises and air-gapped environments as well. That matters for teams whose devices cannot send telemetry to a cloud service. The company also says cost tracking in Tanium Asset indicates where AI software is deployed and what it costs. An endpoint view is useful for these questions, but it is not a substitute for records from browser-based services, cloud systems or the applications an agent uses remotely.

Sources indicate that in the launch announcement, Tanium described a Converge demonstration of a Shadow AI page in Atlas where security teams can see changes in the inventory and ask questions in plain language. The manufacturer described additional aims to rank findings, provide explanations, and tie agent activity to the originating session and prompt. The demonstration and roadmap should not be mistaken for proof that those features are generally available or that they cover every agent or service.

Tanium also looks to let security teams define policies centrally and detect violations before they turn on enforcement. That sequence matters operationally. A local tool that looks unusual in the inventory might be part of a legitimate engineering or accessibility workflow. Reviewing those cases with the people who own the affected systems can help organizations distinguish authorized exceptions from unmanaged software without disrupting routine work.

Sources indicate that the voluntary NIST AI Risk Management Framework puts AI risk in the context of how systems are used, not simply what is installed. For an enterprise, that means linking a device inventory to the people, permissions and business processes behind the entries. It also means deciding what information should be collected and who can review it, especially if future activity records include prompts that may contain confidential work.

The near-term test for AgentSight is whether security teams can keep an accurate inventory as employees adopt and change tools. The more demanding test is whether businesses can connect that visibility to useful decisions: which tools are approved, where an exception is justified, and who should review behavior that falls outside policy. Tanium has shipped the first part of that work. The rest will depend on both the product roadmap and how companies put it to use.

PostgreSQL 19 Released

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Postgresql

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today unveiled the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.
  • It has been revealed that mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale.
  • Sources indicate that "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," mentioned Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today unveiled the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.

It has been revealed that mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale. This release introduces the REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) command so owners can optimize tables for their current workload without disruption to ongoing operations. PostgreSQL 19 gives users better control over blueprint stability and query performance with the fresh pg_plan_advice extension. Developers will find many delightful features in this release, from support for "read-your-writes" consistency on standbys to "get or create" behavior that saves a network round trip.

Sources indicate that "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," mentioned Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team. "PostgreSQL 19 continues that commitment to reliability, giving people new ways to manage their workloads without disruption and to build applications that span multiple systems.".

PostgreSQL, an innovative data management system known for its reliability, robustness, and extensibility, benefits from 30 years of open source development from a global developer community and has become the preferred open source relational database for organizations of all sizes.

Tables that receive many updates and deletes can build up unused space, known as "bloat," which can also significantly impact query performance. The VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands were previously used to handle this, but had tradeoffs, including preventing access to the table until the cleanup finished. PostgreSQL 19 introduces the REPACK command, which reclaims this space and can reorder a table's data to match an index, and with REPACK (CONCURRENTLY), can do so without blocking reads or writes. REPACK replaces the VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands, both of which remain available for compatibility.

According to recent reports, the PostgreSQL query planner usually picks an efficient initiative for each query, but the plan can change as your data changes, and sometimes the newly introduced plan is slower. PostgreSQL 19 adds the pg_plan_advice extension, which allows stabilization of plan choices and the ability to experiment with different plans using the "plan advice" mini-language. The companion pg_stash_advice extension stores advice and automatically applies it to queries based on their query identifier, so you can fix a slow plan without changing your application.

PostgreSQL 19 also helps autovacuum keep up on busy systems. Autovacuum can now vacuum indexes using parallel workers, controlled by the new autovacuum_max_parallel_workers setting, and uses a new scoring system to decide which tables to process first. Queries that read a table can now automatically mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map during execution, reducing the work that future vacuums need to do. Additionally, vacuumdb --analyze-only now analyzes partitioned tables when no tables are specified.

This release adds fresh views for monitoring workloads, including pg_stat_lock for per-lock-type statistics, pg_stat_recovery for recovery status, and pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to show how autovacuum prioritizes tables. The new IO option for EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the matching auto_explain setting report asynchronous I/O activity. PostgreSQL 19 also reports the amount of WAL written for full-page images in pg_stat_wal, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL), and in vacuum and analyze log events.

Recent findings suggest that previously, PostgreSQL often required users to restart their server to enable logical replication, which could be disruptive in production workloads. PostgreSQL 19 simplifies logical replication initialization by automatically raising the effective WAL level to logical when you create the first logical replication slot. You can see the WAL level in use with the new effective_wal_level setting.

In a recent development, postgreSQL 19 also adds logical replication of sequence values, which you can publish using FOR ALL SEQUENCES with CREATE PUBLICATION. CREATE PUBLICATION also adds an EXCEPT clause to exclude tables when publishing FOR ALL TABLES, and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION can now get its connection settings from a foreign server, such as one defined with postgres_fdw, using the SERVER clause. Additionally, the upcoming retain_dead_tuples subscription option lets PostgreSQL detect updates that conflict with a concurrent delete, and these conflicts are counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats.

For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the newly introduced WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

PostgreSQL 19 also improves queries on foreign tables. With the upcoming import_stats option, postgres_fdw can import table statistics from the remote server when you run ANALYZE, instead of sampling rows from the remote table, which helps the query planner choose better plans.

It has been revealed that postgreSQL 19 adds INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, which lets the RETURNING clause return existing rows that conflict with an insert, simplifying the common "get or create" pattern. COPY can now output data as JSON, including as a single JSON array, and the SQL/JSON path language adds string methods such as lower(), upper(), replace(), split_part(), and btrim(). Additionally, the lead(), lag(), first_value(), last_value(), and nth_value() window functions can now skip NULL values using IGNORE NULLS. The random() function can now also generate random dates and timestamps within a range.

Sources indicate that this release also makes many workloads faster without changes to your application. PostgreSQL 19 improves the performance of foreign key checks, which in testing made bulk inserts nearly 2x faster, and adds more query planner optimizations, such as converting NOT IN clauses to more efficient anti-joins when NULL values are not present, and performing eager aggregation before joins to reduce the number of rows to process. PostgreSQL 19 also builds on the asynchronous I/O subsystem added in PostgreSQL 18. When io_method is set to worker (the default), PostgreSQL now automatically adjusts the number of I/O workers between the new io_min_workers and io_max_workers settings, which replace the io_workers setting. There are also scalability improvements when using LISTEN and NOTIFY to exchange notifications in multi-channel workloads.

Finally, the latest password_expiration_warning_threshold setting warns users when their password is about to expire.

Sources indicate that postgreSQL 19 adds server-side support for Server Name Indication (SNI), letting a single PostgreSQL server present a different TLS certificate based on the hostname a client connects to. You can map hostnames to their certificates and keys in the new pg_hosts.conf file. PostgreSQL 19 also now issues a warning after a successful md5 password authentication, which you can turn off with the md5_password_warnings setting. md5 password authentication was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and will be removed in a future release. If you require password-based authentication, use SCRAM authentication. This release also removes support for RADIUS authentication.

According to recent reports, just-in-time compilation (JIT) is now disabled by default, as the cost estimates PostgreSQL used to decide when to use it proved unreliable. If you run many large analytical queries, you may want to enable JIT. When PostgreSQL is built with LZ4 support, the default TOAST compression method is now lz4.

Many other upcoming features and improvements have been added to PostgreSQL 19 that may also be helpful for your use cases. Please see the release notes for a complete list of new and changed features.

It has been revealed that postgreSQL is the world's most advanced open source database, with a global community of thousands of people, contributors, companies and organizations. Since its beginnings at the University of California, Berkeley over 40 years ago, PostgreSQL has continued with an unmatched pace of development. PostgreSQL's mature feature set not only matches top proprietary database systems, but exceeds them in advanced database features, extensibility, security, and stability.

For explanations of the above features and others, please see the following resources:.

There are several ways you can download PostgreSQL 19, including:.

Other tools and extensions are available on the PostgreSQL Extension Network.

PostgreSQL 19 comes with HTML documentation as well as man pages, and you can also browse the documentation online in both HTML and PDF formats.

Industry observers note that postgreSQL uses the PostgreSQL License, a BSD-like "permissive" license. This OSI-certified license is widely appreciated as flexible and business-friendly, since it does not restrict the use of PostgreSQL with commercial and proprietary applications. Together with multi-company support and public ownership of the code, our license makes PostgreSQL very popular with vendors wanting to embed a database in their own products without fear of fees, vendor lock-in, or changes in licensing terms.

In a recent development, postgres, PostgreSQL, and the Elephant Logo (Slonik) are all registered trademarks of the PostgreSQL Community Association. If you wish to use these marks, you must comply with the trademark policy.

It has been revealed that postgreSQL enjoys the support of numerous companies, who sponsor developers, provide hosting resources, and give us financial support. See our sponsors page for some of these project supporters.

There is also a large community of companies offering PostgreSQL Support, from individual consultants to multinational companies.

If you wish to make a financial contribution to the PostgreSQL Global Development Group or one of the recognized community non-profit organizations, please visit our donations page.

#10936. Tech Report: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1280 w)
📖 Baca

Tech Report: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Recent findings suggest that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

Recent findings suggest that after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

According to recent reports, start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

Industry observers note that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

According to recent reports, the table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

It has been revealed that in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

Recent findings suggest that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

In a recent development, the table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Recent findings suggest that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

According to recent reports, key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents.

Nov 20, 2026 6 min read.

In a recent development, AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local implementation of more than 200 of its services dedicated to the public domain under CC0, and states that "thousands of autonomous AI agents wrote every line of code" in it. As InfoQ reported at launch, it ships as a single Rust binary generated from AWS's 438 public API models and listens on port 9297. The week since has brought the first independent fidelity numbers and a divided practitioner reaction.

Pointing an existing SDK, CLI, or coding agent at the emulator is a matter of environment variables, after which the launch post by Daniel Abib says, "your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do":.

It has been revealed that the same shell serves an agent. In the post, Kiro is asked to create and read back a DynamoDB table and issues the ordinary CLI calls against the local endpoint:.

Matt Wood, AWS's chief AI and technology officer, argues that the loop matters because of what an agent does while a check is slow: "A coding agent can build a lot of software around an incorrect assumption." He also names the failure mode an emulator introduces:.

An agent learns from the environment it experiences. If the emulator accepts behavior that AWS rejects, training can reinforce a mistake. An agent might also discover a shortcut that succeeds only because of an emulator defect.

The fidelity scores exist to expose that gap: each release publishes per service how many tests pass out of how many were verified against real AWS, with the failing tests public too, and Abib asks readers to "read a score as a snapshot of a product that's improving.".

Senior principal engineer Matthew Goldberg traces the project to a three-line prompt given to Kiro, "the simplest prompt that I could think of without any expectation that this would work":.

Industry observers note that kiro came back after 15 minutes with a passable first version of an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). I refined my prompt and had Kiro build me the rest of AWS over the weekend. And it did. It obviously had gaps, but it was compelling enough that my team started using it to test our software that Monday.

The production version is built by three agent teams: "One team manages a test suite; one team finds challenges in the emulator; and one team fixes those issues." Each fix must pass a gate that compiles the change and runs agent reviews for coding standards, security, and fidelity regression. "Our team hasn't written or reviewed any of the code," Goldberg writes, and describes what the gate carries:.

If any of those checks fail, the change is sent back to the agent for rework; if they all pass, it is merged to mainline. We've seen thousands of issues fixed every day as hundreds of agents concurrently work on the codebase. Without this merge gate, we wouldn't trust what our agents are building.

Swami Sivasubramanian, in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog, recalls rebuilding a replication engine with Kiro that had taken his team four months by hand:.

I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

In his telling, the engineer's job becomes "to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct.".

The first measurements from outside AWS come from Kento Ikeda, an AWS Community Builder, who ran version 1.0.322 in GitHub Actions the day after launch. DynamoDB, S3 and SQS passed roughly 60 to 70 percent of their fidelity tests at service level and 80 to 100 percent on the operations its code called, while CloudFormation sat near 20 percent. The emulator matched AWS's error wording, but a latest DynamoDB table stayed in CREATING for three seconds and rejected writes until then. "Being generated from API models only means the shape of requests and responses matches AWS," he writes, and places the tool between mocks and a real sandbox as a third layer rather than a replacement for either.

The launch post draws its hardest line at security:.

Don't use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn't evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Industry observers note that unimplemented operations return HTTP 501, telemetry is on by default, throttling, outages and regional differences are not simulated, and the repository does not accept pull requests. On Hacker News, one reader quoted the line on the security page that the emulator "never denies a request signed with its own key" and asked why IAM was left out:.

Sources indicate that I think because the agents were only building on the public API surface, it's hard to build this part. But they should've tried and let the agents read whatever policy engines AWS has. Or maybe it's a way to prevent someone from trivially running aws-emulator as AWSaaS?

The thread's first question was whether this was "just an exercise or a real product they are going to ship and maintain," answered by a commenter identifying as AWS staff with "It's a real product that we plan to maintain." Another counted "29,684 commits in a repository less than a month old" and stated it "does not instill confidence." On r/aws, the most-upvoted comment turned Amazon's own line around, calling agents that fix code "without human review" a terrible idea for a tool used to test before production. The reply was that the API specifications already exist and the SDKs are generated from them, so a server derived from a fixed contract is where agents can iterate until the tests pass.

In a recent development, the timing matters to the people in those threads. LocalStack's free Hobby blueprint now requires an account and prohibits commercial use, with paid seats from $39 a month, and several commenters had already moved to Floci. One of them put the AWS release in that context:.

But in the wake of Localstack's changes, the landscape has been full of slopware and low trust anyway. I don't think this is worse, for now at least.

AWS's version costs nothing and can be forked by either project. Sivasubramanian says AWS "will share more about this work at re:Invent" in December.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Form & Function Consulting has debuted Lever, an AI platform designed to give professional services firms a consistent view of their operations across disconnected systems.
  • The interesting part is not another chatbot answering financial questions.
  • According to the launch announcement, Form & Function starts with information from customer relationship management, professional services automation and finance systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Form & Function Consulting has debuted Lever, an AI platform designed to give professional services firms a consistent view of their operations across disconnected systems. Unveiled on November 12, the product combines operational data with firm-specific business definitions so leaders can ask questions about staffing, revenue forecasts and project profitability through conversational interfaces.

The interesting part is not another chatbot answering financial questions. It is the work required before those answers become useful. A sales system can record a promising deal while a delivery team sees insufficient capacity to fulfill it. An AI assistant needs more than access to both databases to explain what that combination means for the business.

According to the launch announcement, Form & Function starts with information from customer relationship management, professional services automation and finance systems. It also gathers documents and the knowledge employees use to interpret those records. Its Lev chatbot supports stakeholder interviews that capture how a firm actually operates.

That onboarding feeds a context layer describing how work is sold, staffed, delivered and measured. The goal is to connect questions that otherwise fall between departments: whether the sales pipeline supports a hiring decision, which engagements offer the best margins, or how a delayed investment would affect projected cash flow.

This distinction matters in services businesses because similarly named metrics can conceal different assumptions. Available capacity might exclude time spent selling, while a revenue forecast might depend on both a deal’s likelihood of closing and when the resulting work can be delivered. A plausible answer based on the wrong definition can be more misleading than an obvious error.

The company’s Lever product page demonstrates Lev answering questions, generating visual output and working inside Slack. It also indicates access through other AI clients, including Claude and ChatGPT, using Model Context Protocol, or MCP. Rather than requiring every interface to reconstruct the firm’s business logic, the approach supplies a shared foundation for those interactions.

The launch positioned Lever within operating-partner advisory engagements. The current product page also describes standalone availability. Pricing and detailed deployment requirements are not disclosed there, so the announcement should not be read as a self-service rollout with a published subscription price.

The broader move toward shared business meaning is also visible in Collate’s Ontology Studio announcement. Lever takes a narrower approach centered on professional services operations and consultant-assisted onboarding, rather than treating business context as a generic layer that every organization can adopt unchanged.

It has been revealed that form & Function reports that one client identified additional delivery capacity sufficient to support approximately $1.8 million in incremental annual revenue without adding employees. The release also describes an improvement in projected gross margins. Those are potential operating gains identified through analysis, not evidence that the client has already collected that additional revenue.

According to recent reports, the firm’s technical discussion of semantic layers provides more context. In a tech giant-run comparison, it tested five business questions five times each, contrasting access to raw BigQuery data with a semantic model built using Malloy. The structured approach performed better on questions requiring business definitions and relationships between tables.

Sources indicate that that is a useful illustration of the mechanism, but it is a small vendor-run test. It does not establish perfect accuracy across arbitrary questions, changing datasets or every customer’s deployment. Defining metrics in advance reduces ambiguity; it does not eliminate the need to maintain those definitions and review consequential decisions.

Lever’s launch highlights a practical shift in enterprise AI: connecting a model to data is only the beginning. Someone must decide what the data means, resolve conflicting definitions and keep that interpretation current as contracts, staffing policies and business processes change.

According to recent reports, for services firms, the potential benefit is a shorter path from operational records to a decision about capacity or profitability. The lasting test will be whether that shared context stays reliable as the business evolves, and whether identified opportunities turn into measurable results rather than simply more persuasive answers.

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • According to recent reports, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

According to recent reports, in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

Sources indicate that the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

In a recent development, we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

In a recent development, the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

Industry observers note that the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

It has been revealed that the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

Recent findings suggest that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

According to recent reports, this effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Sources indicate that think of a shipping firm that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

It has been revealed that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Sources indicate that adapting a model's vocabulary is not a latest idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

In a recent development, they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

Industry observers note that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Industry observers note that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping organization: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Industry observers note that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

Industry observers note that an expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents highlights up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Industry observers note that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

Industry observers note that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Industry observers note that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.
